meta.title: spec.jev · Only what's needed.
meta.description: spec.jev is a coding agent with a judgment kernel: a small, fast judge called Jev makes dozens of small decisions in every turn, so the task gets only the context it needs. Command line and desktop app, open source.
meta.og_description: A coding agent that gives the task only the context it needs. Built on pi, with Jev as its judge.

home.lead: spec.jev is a coding agent. A small, fast judge called Jev makes dozens of small decisions for the main model in every turn: what stays in the context, whether a command is safe, whether the work is really done. The main model keeps its attention on the work.
home.cli_hint: Needs Node.js 22.19 or newer. Then run spec.jev in a project folder; the first time, spec.jev setup connects a model.
home.app_hint: The macOS app is signed and notarized by Apple; the Windows app isn't signed yet, so SmartScreen shows a warning. The app carries spec.jev inside it: no Node.js to install. Windows on Arm, Linux on Arm and every other download are under Releases.
home.meta: macOS · Windows · Linux · open source (MIT + Apache-2.0) · built on pi
home.story_intro: Ask for a plan, and most agents send every tool and skill description along with it. Models write better code every month, and their reports get harder to read. spec.jev splits the work: Jev judges, the main model works and a model picked for plain speaking tells you where things stand.

chapters.label: When you send a message
chapters.caption: A message comes in; Jev gives a one-line verdict before the main model starts.
paras: Is this a new task, a follow-up or a correction? Should a message that arrives mid-run interrupt now? Does it need skills and tools, or will a one-line answer do?
after: This is a real turn. "{prompt}" comes in, and in under a second Jev answers: a multi-step task, full effort. Skills and MCP servers the task doesn't need stay out of the context until it does.

chapters.label: When a tool answers
chapters.caption: The tests run: 2 of 4 fail.
paras: A test run or a search easily returns hundreds of lines. Jev judges chunk by chunk what matters now; only that enters the context, and the rest is archived behind a pointer, ready when it's needed.
In web pages and MCP results, instructions aimed at the model are withheld before it reads them.

chapters.label: Before acting
chapters.h2: Block what's risky, ask only when it matters
chapters.caption: It finds the cause and fixes one regular expression, without coming back to ask.
paras: Before a command runs, rules flag anything risky, and Jev checks that you asked for it and that it doesn't cross a constraint you stated. There are three permission modes, Full access, Jev approves and Ask first, and you can switch at any time. In Jev approves mode, Jev lets through what the task clearly needs and asks you about the rest.

chapters.label: When the turn ends
chapters.caption: It runs the tests again, all 4 pass and it says what it changed.
paras: When the model says it's done, spec.jev checks whether anything verified that, whether the turn drifted and whether to go back to a checkpoint.

/goal <condition> keeps the agent working until the condition holds. The main model checks whether it does, with Jev as the fallback; when the same error comes back again and again, Jev judges whether the approach is a dead end.

chapters.label: The hive
chapters.h2: Several bees at work, Jev in the middle
paras: When several agents work on one hard problem, splitting up the work is easy; communication is hard. Say nothing, and each walks into the same dead end. Say everything, and every context fills with the others' chatter.

In spec.jev's hive, Jev judges every finding: is it worth sharing, and does it matter to this bee? Only then does it reach another bee as context. When a later finding overturns an earlier one, the correction goes to every bee that heard it.

chapters.label: The plain-language board
chapters.h2: Working and reporting are different jobs
paras: Models get stronger, and their reports read more and more like notes for a machine. In spec.jev the working model keeps working its own way. Every few tool calls Jev checks what happened, picks what's really news and hands it to a model chosen for speaking plainly, which tells you where things stand.
When a run ends, you see not just "done" but what was actually done.

home.principles_intro: A model's attention is limited, and so is its context. These are the things spec.jev chose not to do, or chose to do differently.

principles.p: In Jev approves mode, Jev lets through what the task clearly needs and asks you about the rest.
Each message is judged: small talk, a follow-up or work to do. Skills and MCP servers that aren't needed stay out of the context.
When the context grows, stale tool results are dropped instead of summarized, and summary-free compaction is an option. Before the cache expires, spec.jev judges whether a refresh is worth it.
{points} decision points, each with its own switch and its own judge: the free Jev, the local Laya or any LLM.
Without a judge key, the free Jev on OpenCode Zen answers, and spec.jev says so once a day.
The command line is built on pi, with its models, extensions, skills and session tree; the desktop app is built on AionUi.

more.text: Bring in your Codex and Claude Code conversations and carry on in spec.jev.
ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Google, signed in inside the app, no keys to copy around.
Your corrections and the traps the agent found a way around are kept; a lesson that is recalled and never followed retires itself.
Jev drives it step by step: look at the page, judge once, act; it stops to ask before submitting or paying.
Every verdict and how long it took: /status, spec.jev ledger and the app's Judge tab.
The desktop app speaks English, 简体中文, 繁體中文, 日本語, 한국어 and 8 more.
